profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a SaaS product company’s internal developer-experience group. The team wants to use findings from the paper on agile requirements engineering practices in Brazilian software companies to plan a lightweight internal study and an accompanying guidance memo for product squads that have struggled with backlog refinement and user-story quality. The context is that leadership asked for a two-week plan that can quickly produce actionable insights without starting a full research program. The agenda is to agree on what the 'survey' deliverable includes, which teams will be sampled, how evidence will be collected, who owns execution, and what timeline checkpoints mean. The expected outcome is a shared plan for running the internal study and drafting a recommendation memo for engineering managers and product managers.

members.name: Camila Rocha
members.expertise: Agile delivery processes, cross-team coordination, internal tooling adoption
members.background: Camila leads a platform-adjacent team that supports engineering effectiveness across six product squads; she previously worked as a scrum master and later as an EM in a fintech where lightweight internal process assessments were common.
members.private_state: She wants a credible plan that looks research-informed but can be executed with minimal disruption to delivery teams, and she is especially concerned about producing something leadership can circulate within two weeks.
hidden_assumptions: A 'survey' for this kind of internal planning can include a short questionnaire plus a few follow-up interviews under the same workstream.
The 'pilot squads' naturally means the three product squads already flagged by engineering directors as having recurring backlog-quality issues.
A 'draft by Friday' means a leadership-ready document in the company’s shared template by end of day local time so review can start over the weekend queue.
If they 'capture current practices,' it is reasonable to include adjacent artifacts like refinement notes, acceptance criteria examples, and ticket templates from the selected squads.

members.name: Rafael Mendes
members.expertise: Internal research operations, process measurement, survey design, reporting
members.background: Rafael supports PM and engineering leadership with internal process diagnostics; he has a background in business analytics and has run several company-wide pulse surveys but fewer interview-based studies.
members.private_state: He wants the plan to stay tightly scoped and methodologically clean so he can execute it with existing ops bandwidth and avoid opening a qualitative research effort he cannot staff.
hidden_assumptions: A 'survey' means a structured questionnaire only, with standardized response options and no interviews unless separately approved.
The 'pilot squads' means all squads in the product organization will receive the questionnaire, with analysis later focused on whichever groups respond sufficiently.
A 'draft by Friday' means an internal working draft can be uploaded any time before midnight UTC because leadership review will not start until next week anyway.
When they say 'collection and specification practices,' they are only talking about how teams elicit and write requirements, not about gathering artifact samples or reviewing historical tickets.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'run a survey' based on the paper.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Camila means a mixed lightweight package: a short questionnaire plus a few follow-up conversations to flesh out how squads collect and specify requirements.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Rafael means a questionnaire-only instrument with standardized answers, because that is what makes it a survey operationally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the legitimate umbrella term 'survey' in an internal planning setting, and mixed-method follow-ups often feel like a minor implementation detail rather than a separate methodological decision.

misalignment_points.topic: Which squads are in the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with the 'pilot squads.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Camila is referring to the three squads already discussed in prior leadership meetings: Atlas, Billing Core, and Onboarding.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Rafael is referring to the first wave of respondents across the whole product organization, expecting all squads to receive the questionnaire and only later identifying a pilot subset analytically.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have recently heard the phrase 'pilot squads' in adjacent conversations, so each treats the referent as already shared context and sees no need to restate the names.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in documenting current practices
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'document current collection and specification practices.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Camila includes reviewing real squad artifacts such as backlog templates, acceptance criteria snippets, and refinement notes to ground the recommendations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Rafael limits this to self-reported practices captured through questionnaire responses, excluding artifact review as outside scope.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds routine and complete on its own, and both see artifact handling as an obvious extension or non-extension of 'documenting practices' rather than a separate scope boundary to negotiate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have a 'draft by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Camila believes this means a leadership-ready draft in the standard memo format, polished enough to circulate by Friday 5 PM São Paulo time.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Rafael believes this means a rough internal draft with preliminary charts and notes uploaded before 00:00 UTC, not yet ready for circulation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning meetings, 'draft by Friday' often sounds sufficiently specific; each person silently fills in their own normal standard for readiness and timing without feeling any ambiguity.

turns.inner_thought: Leadership wants something they can circulate fast, not an open-ended study. If we anchor it in that Brazilian paper, it will sound solid, but I need the work to stay lightweight. For me, run a survey means a short questionnaire and then a handful of follow-up conversations so we get enough texture to write practical guidance. And draft by Friday needs to mean a polished memo in the shared template by end of day here, otherwise we lose the weekend review window.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Leadership asked for a fast plan, and they specifically want it grounded in that Brazilian agile requirements survey rather than us inventing a whole new framework. I’d like us to lock the approach for the internal survey and the companion memo within the next two weeks, and ideally have a draft by Friday so we keep momentum.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as we keep this operationally clean. I can stand up a questionnaire quickly if we mirror the paper’s categories and avoid interviews or any extra qualitative layer. Document current collection and specification practices should come straight from structured responses; otherwise this balloons beyond available ops bandwidth.
turns.utterance: That sounds workable. I can get the survey moving quickly if we keep the instrument tight and borrow the paper’s main themes—how teams handle collection methods, specification practices, perceived benefits, and the main difficulties they run into. That should give us a clean base for the memo.

turns.inner_thought: We should absolutely start with Atlas, Billing Core, and Onboarding since directors already flagged them and we can get meaningful examples fast. When I say pilot squads, Rafael will know the set from leadership context, so no need to relist them.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I think we should start with the pilot squads so we can get richer input first before we decide whether anything needs to go broader.

turns.inner_thought: Makes sense to use pilot squads as the initial response wave across product and then analyze whichever groups give us enough usable data. I’ll distribute broadly to the product org and monitor completion; that gives me a better shot at stable patterns without committing to a bigger phase yet.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works for me. I’ll distribute to the pilot squads first and keep an eye on response volume so we have enough data to summarize patterns with some confidence.

turns.inner_thought: We can’t write a credible memo from checkbox data alone. Besides the survey package, I want us to document current collection and specification practices by pulling a few real artifacts—refinement notes, acceptance criteria examples, ticket templates—from those squads. That’s still lightweight and gives leadership something concrete.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want us to include: besides the survey, we should document current collection and specification practices so the memo reflects how teams actually work today, not just the abstract themes from the paper.

turns.inner_thought: Right, we can capture that directly in the questionnaire. If I structure the form well, respondents can tell us how they collect and specify requirements and where the friction is. That keeps everything standardized and avoids creating a parallel evidence stream I’d have to manage.
turns.utterance: Makes sense. I’d structure the form so people can indicate which elicitation and specification techniques they use, how consistently they use them, and what challenges they report. That should let us document current collection and specification practices in a pretty usable way.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll handle the squad leads directly and ask for examples from Atlas, Billing Core, and Onboarding—recent user stories, backlog refinement outputs, maybe a couple of acceptance criteria snippets. That will let us ground the recommendations without dragging teams into a big process exercise.
turns.utterance: Great. I can also reach out to the squad leads for examples from backlog refinement and recent user stories, just so the recommendations are grounded in concrete practice from the pilot squads.

turns.inner_thought: If she talks to leads informally, fine—that may help us interpret odd response patterns. My part stays straightforward: survey build, response tracking, summary tables. I’m still treating the survey as the core evidence source and documenting practices through self-report, not artifact review.
turns.utterance: That should help with interpretation. I’ll own the survey build, response tracking, and the summary tables, and then we can line that up with the way we document current collection and specification practices.

turns.inner_thought: I need something polished enough to package immediately. If he gets me inputs by Friday afternoon, I can shape the narrative and send a leadership-ready memo before close of business São Paulo time. I’m assuming he’s aligned on that standard of readiness.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Then let’s aim for a draft by Friday so I can package the findings and recommendations for leadership review right away.

turns.inner_thought: That’s fine. A working draft uploaded before midnight UTC is realistic—some early charts, a short write-up, and notes on what the responses show. Leadership won’t really look until next week, so we don’t need final polish by then.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do a draft by Friday. Once responses are in, I can have the initial analysis and write-up uploaded so you’ve got something to work from.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I’ll own outreach to the three named squads and shape the memo framing. Rafael will prepare the survey materials and synthesis, and I’m assuming that includes the short follow-up layer and enough substance for a circulation-ready Friday draft.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll take squad outreach and memo framing, and you can prepare the survey materials and the synthesis. That should give us a clean split and keep the survey moving without a lot of overhead.

turns.inner_thought: Clear enough: I’ll launch the questionnaire to the pilot squads as I understand them, track the data coming in, and send over the Friday draft once the initial cut is uploaded. This stays contained and executable with current bandwidth.
turns.utterance: Done. I’ll launch to the pilot squads, collect the data, and send over the Friday draft. If anything looks off in the response pattern, I’ll flag it early so we can still keep the timeline.
